title: The People's Watch · November 2026: the 2026-Q3 reading
subtitle: Watching a proposed money rule run in public, every month.
subject: The rule's 2026-Q3 call: 2.23% (and a money myth, busted)
preview: Prices vs. target, the brake, and what the watchers saw.
html:
The official reading for 2026-Q3 is in, and the short story is this: prices drifted a little above the rule's target, so it eased money growth to 2.23% a year. Here's what that means, what the watchers saw, and one money myth worth retiring.

The short version

  • This quarter's official reading is in. For 2026-Q3, prices sat 0.47 log points (about 0.47%) above the target, so the rule would let money grow 2.23% a year.

  • The brake is off: prices are nowhere near high enough to need it.

  • The watchers: dollar trouble abroad reads calm, home financial stress reads calm, and the money plumbing reads calm.

  • We attacked our own record 10 ways. Every attack was caught.

The number this quarter

Think of the rule as a thermostat for the dollar. Every quarter, on a fixed date, it reads the official price data and decides how fast the supply of public money may grow.

  • Prices vs. the flat target: 0.47 log points (about 0.47%) above the target, measured from where prices stood when the shadow run began (2026-Q2).

  • The economy's long-run growth: 2.47% a year (real GDP, ten-year average).

  • So the rule allows: 2.47% minus half the price gap = 2.23% a year, kept between 0% and 4%.

  • Checked three ways: three separately written calculators all got the same answer.

Prices drifted above target, so the rule eases off a little, the way a thermostat clicks the heat down when the room runs warm. Nothing is executed and no dollar amount is published; this is a public test run.

Your dollar, then and now

Here's what inflation has done to a dollar saved at different times, by the government's own price index (CPI-U, through October 2026):

  • A dollar saved in January 2000 buys about 50¢ of goods today.

  • A dollar saved in January 2020 buys about 77¢.

The book's goal is a dollar that still buys about the same when your grandchildren spend it. Whether a rule can deliver that is what this experiment is testing.

What the watchers saw

Our sentinels never act; they just keep watch around the clock, like smoke detectors. Here's what they read this month:

  • Emergency dollar loans to foreign central banks: $0.17 billion outstanding (calm). In the 2020 panic they peaked near $449 billion.

  • Treasuries held for foreign governments at the Fed: down 2.8% over 13 weeks (calm). A fast drop can mean foreign holders are raising dollars.

  • The dollar against other currencies: up 0.5% over about a month (calm). A sudden jump is the classic sign of a dollar squeeze abroad.

  • Overnight borrowing costs: 0.00 points above the rate the Fed pays banks (calm). When this spikes, cash is getting scarce.

  • What markets expect for inflation in the long run: 2.18% a year (calm).

  • Overall financial stress (St. Louis Fed index): -0.49, where 0 is normal (calm).

Myth or fact? "Woodrow Wilson said, 'I have unwittingly ruined my country.'"

Never said. This quote is everywhere online, but there is no record of Wilson saying it. Repeating it hands defenders of the current system an easy way to dismiss everything else. The accurate history is strong enough on its own.

Source: The People's Money, Ch. 2

This month in money history

The secret meeting that was real

In November 1910, a handful of the most powerful bankers in America slipped away to a private club on Jekyll Island, Georgia, traveling under first names only, to draft a banking plan. One of them, Frank Vanderlip, later admitted he had been 'as secretive, indeed, as furtive as any conspirator.' What they drafted became the blueprint for the Federal Reserve.

Source: Vanderlip, From Farm Boy to Financier (1935)

Kitchen-table explainer: What's a digital fingerprint?

Every file the system downloads gets a fingerprint (a 'hash'): a short code that changes completely if even one digit in the file changes. It works like a wax seal on an old letter. If the seal doesn't match, someone opened it.

We tried to break it

Before every run, a red-team agent attacks a throwaway copy of the public record: forging the ledger, editing the data, making a calculator lie, trying to escape the sandbox. This month: 10 of 10 attacks caught. Every run's fingerprint is also handed to three outside witnesses we don't control: the Bitcoin blockchain, a public transparency log, and the Internet Archive. Our latest checkpoint is sealed in Bitcoin block 975811.

From the community: Purchasing-power clock, by People's Money project (example agent): A dollar saved in January 2000 now buys about 50¢ (CPI-U, 2026-10)

What we still don't know

Whether the rule would actually keep prices steady. What credit and mortgages would cost. Whether the switch could happen without serious disruption. Whether a cheaper reform could get most of the benefit. Those are the tests in Chapter 9, and we will report them, good or bad, as they come in.

See the live record

The People's Watch is an unofficial, public shadow run of the money rule proposed in The People's Money by Jamie Murray. It executes nothing, publishes no dollar issuance figure, and has not shown that the rule keeps prices stable; those tests are still ahead. Not financial advice.
